title: Honi and the carob tree
hookLine: an old man plants a tree that won't fruit for seventy years, for his grandchildren (Talmud, Taanit 23a)

lines: AN OLD MAN PLANTING A TREE.
cards: Somebody planted the tree whose shade you last sat in. Somebody laid out the park, stocked the library, worked out the recipe a family still makes, knowing they would never meet the people who'd use it.
The Talmud has a story about this, and about a man named Honi.
Tradition remembers him as a holy man in the land of Israel, Honi the Circle-Drawer, because once, in a drought, he drew a circle on the ground and would not step out of it until it rained.
One day Honi is walking along a road, and he sees an old man planting a tree.

teach.h: WE WERE LIKE THEM THAT DREAM.
teach.b: It begins with a verse that bothered Honi, from a psalm about the return from exile. In the King James words: "When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream."
Seventy years in exile, like a dream. Can a person really sleep seventy years? So Honi is on the road, turning that over, when he sees the old man planting a carob tree.
How long until this tree gives fruit? Seventy years, says the man.

teach.h: ARE YOU SURE YOU'LL LIVE SEVENTY YEARS?
teach.b: Are you so sure you'll live another seventy years? And the old man says, more or less: I found carob trees in the world when I came into it.
My ancestors planted them for me. So I'm planting these for my children. Then Honi sits down to eat, and falls asleep.
Rocks grow up around him, hiding him, and he sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that same tree. Are you the one who planted it?
I'm his grandson. The story ends sadly: back home, nobody believes he's Honi, and he feels so alone that he no longer wants to live.
The rabbis draw a saying from it: companionship or death. But the heart of the first part is the old man, planting. He does the work, and the fruit belongs to someone he'll never meet.
He got here under trees he didn't plant, and he knows it.

how: Jews read the story of Honi in the Talmud, Taanit 23a, and it is a familiar retelling around Tu BiShvat, the new year of the trees.

o: the olive, a tree that lives for centuries
the fig, a tree of shade and peace at home
the carob, a tree that is slow to bear fruit

games.q: you're the old man, planting a carob tree that won't give fruit for seventy years. a stranger asks if you expect to live that long. what do you say?
o: my ancestors planted for me, so I plant for my children.
I'll sell the tree before then.
games.why: he found carob trees in the world when he came, so he plants for those after him. seventy years later, his grandson gathers the fruit.

practice: Look around and find one thing near you that someone made or planted before you, a tree outside, a building, a word you use, and thank them silently, whoever they were.
Then think of one small thing you could start for someone after you: a seed in a pot, a note for your kids, money set aside, a skill you teach.
